title: Common mistakes
sub: Overflow, boundaries, modifying a collection in a loop, strings and char, comparers — and how to check code by hand in a minute
cards/0/body:
int runs from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647, about ±2.1·10⁹. By default C# computes unchecked: when a value crosses the limit it silently wraps around, int.MaxValue + 1 == int.MinValue. No exception — just a wrong answer.

Where it bites in interviews:

Sums. 10⁵ numbers up to 10⁹ add up to 10¹⁴ — sum in a long.
Products. long x = a * b; still overflows: the multiplication happens in int, and widening comes after. You need (long)a * b.
The middle. (lo + hi) / 2 overflows when lo + hi > int.MaxValue: on arrays larger than 2³⁰ elements or in a binary search over values up to 2·10⁹. The safe form is lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
Absolute value. Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws OverflowException, and -int.MinValue equals int.MinValue again.

checked { … } turns overflow into an exception — handy in tests, so the bug does not hide.
cards/0/code:
int a = 100_000, b = 100_000;
long wrong = a * b;              // 1410065408: multiplied in int, widened afterwards
long right = (long)a * b;        // 10000000000

int lo = 1_500_000_000, hi = 2_000_000_000;
int bad = (lo + hi) / 2;         // a negative number
int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;    // 1750000000

checked { int boom = int.MaxValue + a; }  // OverflowException instead of a silent bug
cards/0/deep:
“Infinity” in distances. dist[v] = int.MaxValue as “not reached yet” — and dist[v] + w wraps into a negative number that looks like the best path. Either check dist[v] != int.MaxValue before adding, use int.MaxValue / 2, or use long.

Checking across the project. The CheckForOverflowUnderflow property in the .csproj makes checked the default — useful in debug builds and tests. Then, where overflow is intended (hashes, random number generators), write unchecked.

Where to get more width. long goes up to 9.2·10¹⁸, ulong up to 1.8·10¹⁹. Beyond that there is System.Numerics.BigInteger (Unity has it too), but in an interview you are usually expected to notice the overflow and avoid it with a formula or by working modulo something.
cards/1/q: a[i] and b[i] are up to 10⁶, the length is up to 10⁵. On large inputs the sum sometimes comes out negative. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/1/explain: a[i] * b[i] is up to 10¹², and the multiplication happens in int: the result wraps before it is ever added to the long. You need (long)a[i] * b[i]. The sum itself is up to 10¹⁷, which fits in a long.
cards/2/body:
The off-by-one error is the most common one in interviews. The cure is to pick one convention for boundaries and stick to it across the whole solution.

Half-open [lo, hi): lo is included, hi is not. The length is hi − lo, an empty range is lo == hi, and halving gives [lo, mid) and [mid, hi) with no gaps or overlaps. This is how for (i = 0; i < n; i++), Span.Slice and most APIs work.
Closed [lo, hi]: both ends are included — hi = n − 1, a while (lo <= hi) loop, moves to mid + 1 and mid − 1, as in the binary search from the first lesson. A closed range [a, b] holds b − a + 1 elements, not b − a: that is how you count windows and iterations too.

Mixing conventions gives an infinite loop or a lost element. Another C# trap: the second argument of Substring(start, length), Slice, Array.Copy and GetRange is a length, not an end index as in Java or Python. The check is the boundary iterations: what happens on the first, on the last, and with n = 0.
cards/3/q: You need to go through every substring of length k in a string of length n. Which loop condition on the start i is right, and how many windows are there?
cards/3/options/0: i <= n - k; n − k + 1 windows
cards/3/options/1: i < n - k; n − k windows
cards/3/options/3: i <= n - k + 1; n − k + 2 windows
cards/3/explain: The last window starts at n − k and ends at n − 1. The starts run from 0 to n − k inclusive, n − k + 1 of them. Check the edge case k = n: there is exactly one window, i = 0, and the condition 0 <= 0 lets it through.
cards/3/wrong/1: It loses the last window, the one that starts at n − k. With k = n the loop does not run at all, although there is one window.
cards/3/wrong/2: Windows that start after n − k run past the end of the string, and Substring throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
cards/3/wrong/3: With i = n − k + 1 the window ends at index n — past the end of the string.
cards/4/body:
The enumerators of List<T>, HashSet<T> and Dictionary remember the collection’s version number. Add and Remove change it, and the next step of foreach throws InvalidOperationException: “Collection was modified”. How to remove correctly:

1. list.RemoveAll(e => e.Hp <= 0) — one pass, O(n), order preserved.
2. A for loop from the end with RemoveAt(i): the indices of elements not yet visited do not shift. But every removal from the middle is a shift, O(n²) in the worst case.
3. From the end, swapping with the last element (the trick from the collections lesson) — O(1) per removal, order changes.
4. For a dictionary, collect the keys into a separate list, then remove them.

A forward for loop with RemoveAt(i) throws nothing but skips the next element: it moved into the removed one’s place while i moved on. “Then and now”: since .NET Core 3.0 you may call Remove and Clear on a Dictionary during foreach, but do not rely on it in .NET Framework or in Unity.
cards/5/q: How do you correctly remove dead enemies from a List<Enemy>? Select every correct way.
cards/5/options/0: A for loop from the end with RemoveAt(i)
cards/5/options/2: foreach over enemies with enemies.Remove(e) inside
cards/5/options/3: A forward for loop with RemoveAt(i), without adjusting i
cards/5/options/4: A loop from the end: put the last element in place of i and remove the last
cards/5/explain: Removing from the end does not shift what is still ahead. RemoveAll makes one pass and keeps the order. Swapping with the last element is O(1) per removal when order does not matter. foreach with Remove throws InvalidOperationException on the next step, and a forward loop without adjusting i skips the element that moved into the removed one’s place.
cards/6/body:
Some .NET string operations are culture-sensitive by default — they compare by the language rules of the current machine: CompareTo, string.Compare(a, b), StartsWith(string), EndsWith(string), IndexOf(string), and also Array.Sort and List.Sort on strings and OrderBy(s => s). Whereas ==, Equals, Contains(string) and IndexOf(char) are ordinal: they compare character codes.

Why that is a bug in an algorithm: the sort order depends on the machine, in the Turkish culture “I” and “i” are not an upper/lower case pair, and linguistic comparison is several times slower. Since .NET 5, Windows too uses the ICU library for culture, and, for example, "\r\n".IndexOf("\n") started returning −1 even though the character is there. In string problems, pass StringComparison.Ordinal or StringComparer.Ordinal explicitly.
cards/7/body:
A char in C# is a 16-bit number, a UTF-16 code unit. That gives both tricks and traps.

Letter index: c - 'a' is an int from 0 to 25 if c is a lowercase Latin letter. Digit: '7' - '0' == 7. Back again: (char)('a' + k) — without the cast you get a number.
Arithmetic yields int: 'a' + 1 is 98, and Console.Write('a' + 1) prints 98. The expression is evaluated left to right, so "" + 'a' + 1 is "a1": the string comes first and everything is appended to it.
Not just Latin: char.IsLetter lets “é” through, and counts[c - 'a'] goes out of the bounds of an int[26]. Emoji and some CJK characters are two chars (a surrogate pair), so s.Length counts code units, not characters.

That is why “lowercase Latin only?” is a mandatory question at the clarification step. If not, use a Dictionary<char, int> or a dictionary keyed by code points.
cards/7/code:
int idx = 'k' - 'a';             // 10
int digit = '7' - '0';           // 7
char next = (char)('a' + 1);     // 'b'
Console.Write('a' + 1);          // 98 — the addition produced an int
Console.Write("" + 'a' + 1);     // a1 — the string comes first
Console.Write("😀".Length);      // 2: a surrogate pair
cards/8/explain: The expression is evaluated left to right: 'a' + 1 adds a char and an int, giving the int 98. Then 98 + "b" is concatenation with a string: "98b". To get "bb" you need (char)('a' + 1) + "b".
cards/8/wrong/1: "a1" would come out if the string were first. Here 'a' + 1 comes first, and that is arithmetic, not concatenation.
cards/8/wrong/2: 'a' + 1 is the int 98, not the char 'b': without a (char) cast there is no letter.
cards/8/wrong/3: It all compiles: char + int gives an int, and int + string gives a string.
cards/9/body:
The a - b comparer is a classic bug. While the numbers are small it works, but the difference of numbers with large magnitudes overflows: 2·10⁹ − (−2·10⁹) does not fit in an int and turns negative, and the comparer lies about the order. The result is a wrong sort, and sometimes an exception saying “IComparer.Compare() method returns inconsistent results”. The right way is a.CompareTo(b): it only compares, no subtraction.

Stability. Array.Sort and List<T>.Sort in .NET are an introspective sort: O(n log n) in the worst case, but unstable — elements with equal keys may swap places. If the original order of equals matters (events at the same time, players with the same score), there are two ways: LINQ OrderBy and ThenBy — stable, but they allocate; or add the original index to the key.

Several keys: compare by the first and, on a tie, by the second. Tuples do it for you: (a.Time, a.Id).CompareTo((b.Time, b.Id)).
cards/9/deep:
Introspective sort. It starts as a quicksort with a median-of-three pivot; ranges of up to 16 elements are finished with insertion sort; if the recursion depth exceeds about 2·log₂ n (bad pivots), it switches to heapsort. That is why the worst case is O(n log n) rather than the O(n²) of plain quicksort. .NET Framework has done this since 4.5; before that Array.Sort was a quicksort with a quadratic worst case.

API variants. Array.Sort(keys, items) sorts two arrays in parallel — keys and the data attached to them, with no tuples. Span<T>.Sort exists since .NET 5; Unity does not have it. Unity.Collections provides NativeArray<T>.Sort() for Jobs and Burst data.

Why LINQ is stable. OrderBy first computes the keys into a separate array and, on equal keys, compares the original positions. The price is arrays of keys and indices, an iterator and a delegate: hot code in Unity does not use it.
cards/10/q: Merging intervals. On tests with large-magnitude coordinates the result is sometimes wrong. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/10/explain: x[0] − y[0] with x[0] = 2·10⁹ and y[0] = −2·10⁹ is 4·10⁹, which overflows into a negative: the comparer calls the larger number smaller, and the sort breaks. The rest of the code is right as long as the intervals are sorted by start. You need x[0].CompareTo(y[0]).
cards/11/title: Empty input, one element, recursion depth: a one-minute check
cards/11/body:
Before you say “done”, walk the code through a short list. It takes a minute and catches most interview bugs.

1. Empty input and a single element — will a[0], a[n − 1], res[res.Count − 1] blow up?
2. Two equal, all equal, all different.
3. Boundaries: the answer at the first and at the last position, a distance of exactly k, a condition like i <= n − k.
4. Signs and sizes: negatives, zero, maximum values — is int enough?
5. “Not found”: what is returned when the loop ends.
6. Recursion depth on the maximum input: up to 10⁶ on a 1000×1000 grid, and then you need an explicit stack (the C# and Unity lesson).

Do the dry run on the smallest non-trivial example and write the variables down in a column after each iteration — that shows both the boundaries and the order of operations. Tests in code are short checks for these cases.
cards/12/q: Match the bug with its fix.
cards/12/pairs/4/1: RemoveAll or a loop from the end
